title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Diabetes
Diabetes is a metabolic disease characterized by high blood glucose levels known as hyperglycemia.1,2 The most common forms of chronic diabetes are type 1 diabetes (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D).1 T1D is an autoimmune disease characterized by the destruction of the pancreatic islet \(\beta\)-cells, leading to an absolute insulin deficiency.3 T2D is the most common form of diabetes and in contrast to T1D it generally begins with insulin resistance in which the body’s cells become less responsive to insulin.1,4 Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting glucose uptake in insulin-sensitive tissues, particularly skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, and by stimulating glycogen synthesis in the liver. As an anabolic hormone, insulin also promotes energy storage and may contribute to weight gain.5 Initially, the pancreas compensates by increasing insulin secretion, however over time progressive \(\beta\)-cell dysfunction results in inadequate insulin production to meet the body’s demands.1,2,4 Despite their distinct underlying pathophysiology, both T1D and T2D are characterized by chronic hyperglycemia.
Diabetes can be diagnosed based on a bloodtest to check hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) levels or through plasma glucose criteria (Table 1.1).3,6
Although both plasma glucose tests and HbA1c measurements are appropriate for diabetes screening, the HbA1c measurement has several advantages.3 Some of the benefits are that it requires no fasting and it is less sensitive to stress and changes in nutrition.3 HbA1c is an indirect measure of blood glucose levels because glucose binds to hemoglobin over \(\sim\) 120 days lifespan of erythrocytes (red blood cells).3 However HbA1c testing is not always accessible, affordable or suitable (e.g., for people with anemia or under HIV-treatment).3

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 Blood Glucose Monitoring
A common treatment goal for non-pregnant adults with diabetes is for HbA1c to be below 53 mmol/mol and not have any hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia (low blood glucose levels).7,8 This corresponds to an estimated average glucose of 8.6 mmol/L.7 However HbA1c goals should be individualized to fit each individual’s specific situation and may be higher or lower than 53 mmol/mol.7,8 There are two tools available for self-assessment of glycemia, the self-monitoring blood glucose (SMBG) device measuring capillary blood with finger-sticks, and the continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) device measuring interstitial fluid (fluid around and between cells) continuously.8,9 Both monitoring devices have shown to improve glycemic control in people with diabetes, however the CGM devices are superior when it comes to immediate information and alerts on asymptomatic hypo- and hyperglycemic events and provide a comprehensive glucose profile including both pre- and postprandial blood glucose measurements.8,10,11

1.2.1 Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Automated Insulin Delivery
The CGM devices measure the glucose in the interstitial fluid, which corresponds with plasma glucose although a lag can appear when glucose levels rise or fall rapidly.12 Use of CGM devices has shown to improve glycemic control in both T1D and T2D with improvements in HbA1c levels and more time spent in target range (standard: 3.9-10 mmol/L) regardless of age, sex, eduction and income.7,12 CGM devices focus on monitoring and it is possible to get an ambulatory glucose profile (AGP) report from the devices (Figure 1.1). The AGP report shows summary statistics over all data (usually a two weeks period) including CGM-derived metrics as shown in (Table 1.2).10 Besides monitoring, data from CGM devices are now used in combination with insulin delivery systems to automate the process of administering insulin.12 automated insulin delivery (AID) systems typically use data from CGM devices to determine or adjust insulin delivery. The simplest AIDs are threshold-based low-glucose suspend systems in which insulin delivery is automatically suspended when blood glucose levels drop below a predefined threshold.13 AID systems are becoming increasingly sophisticated, with the long-term goal of approximating the physiological regulation of glucose by a healthy pancreas. However, the delayed onset and peak action of subcutaneously administered insulin limit the ability of these systems to respond rapidly to changing glucose concentrations.14 Consequently, accurate short-term glucose forecasting has become increasingly important, particularly for anticipating postprandial glucose excursions and enabling earlier insulin adjustments to reduce the risk of both hyper- and hypoglycemia.14 More advanced systems are beginning to utilize additional information such as carbohydrate intake and physical activity to optimize insulin delivery.15,16

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Glycemic Control and Variability
A challenge in achieving good glycemic control is keeping blood glucose levels low enough to reduce the risk of long-term complications, while avoiding hypoglycemia, which can cause acute symptoms and, in insulin-treated individuals, may be life-threatening.17 The variability in the blood glucose fluctuations needs to be reduced in order to lower the average blood glucose levels while still avoiding hypoglycemia.17 Advances in CGM technology have enabled the quantification of glucose variability, a measure of the extent of fluctuations in blood glucose levels over time, including both peaks and nadirs.18 Describing the variability is important because two individuals with similar HbA1c levels may exhibit different glycemic variability profiles.17 Numerous metrics have been developed to characterize different aspects of glucose variability, but no single measure captures all of its dimensions. Although international consensus recommendations advocate the routine reporting of glucose variability using coefficient of variation (CV), mean amplitude of glycemic excursions (MAGE), and standard deviation (SD), with particular emphasis on CV,10 glucose variability encompasses multiple dimensions, including within- and between-day variability, the amplitude of glucose excursions, and temporal glucose patterns.17 As a result, no single metric has been shown to comprehensively capture all aspects of glucose variability, and no consensus currently exists regarding the optimal measure.17,18

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Cardiovascular Diseases and Heart Failure
Although advances in diabetes management have reduced the incidence of several diabetes-related complications, cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in people with diabetes.19–21 Chronic hyperglycemia can lead to long-term complications such as atherosclerotic CVD, although the progression and manifestation of these complications vary between individuals.3 Identifying individuals at increased risk of CVD or heart failure before clinical disease develops is therefore an important component of diabetes care.20
Heart failure is at least twice as prevalent among people with diabetes as in the general population.20,22 It is characterized by symptoms such as breathlessness, fatigue, and ankle swelling, which may be accompanied by clinical signs such as elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary crackles, and peripheral oedema.23 Heart failure may present as either acute or chronic, with acute heart failure typically involving rapid onset or worsening of symptoms and signs.23 In individuals with suspected chronic heart failure based on risk factors, symptoms, clinical findings, and supporting investigations such as electrocardiography, measurement of natriuretic peptides, including N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), is recommended as part of the diagnostic work-up.23 An NT-proBNP concentration of ≥125 pg/mL or higher indicates the need for further cardiac evaluation, whereas concentrations below this threshold make chronic heart failure unlikely and alternative diagnoses should be considered.23 Although NT-proBNP levels may be influenced by non-cardiac factors, including age, ischemic stroke, and renal dysfunction,23 it remains clinically useful in the assessment of individuals at increased risk of chronic heart failure.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Models
To facilitate early identification of individuals at increased cardiovascular risk, several clinical prediction models have been developed.21,24–26 By estimating the probability of a CVD event within a specified time horizon, these models can increase awareness of cardiovascular risk, encourage adherence to recommended lifestyle changes and medical treatment, and help identify individuals who are most likely to benefit from preventive interventions.27 Among these, the Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation 2-Diabetes (SCORE2-Diabetes) model estimates the 10-year risk of CVD in individuals with T2D. It was developed and calibrated using European cohorts, making it particularly relevant for the Danish cohort included in this dissertation.21 However, the SCORE2-Diabetes model relies solely on traditional clinical variables, including age, sex, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL cholesterol), age at diabetes diagnosis, HbA1c, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and does not incorporate information on glucose dynamics beyond the long-term glycemic exposure reflected by HbA1c.21 HbA1c has been independently associated with risk of heart failure,28 however it does not capture the short-term glucose fluctuations, which may be associated with the progression of vascular complications in diabetes.29

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.6 Association vs Prediction
Association and prediction are distinct analytical objectives, although the terms are sometimes used interchangeably in the medical literature. However the distinction is necessary because associations do not necessarily imply predictive utility.30 Association studies aim to identify relationships between variables and an outcome at group level, whereas prediction models are developed to estimate future outcomes for individual patients.30
Traditional statistical association modelling is often used to test hypotheses regarding associations between exposures, \(X\) and outcomes, \(Y\).31 Regression models applied to observational data are commonly used to evaluate hypotheses derived from prior knowledge, where the choice of exposures is guided by existing theory.31 These approaches are based on the premise that the chosen statistical model adequately represents the underlying data-generating mechanism, allowing conclusions to be drawn from the estimated model parameters.32 Results from association studies are typically summarized using estimated effect measures, such as regression coefficients, odds ratios, hazard ratios, or risk ratios, together with confidence intervals and significance tests.30
In contrast, prediction modelling applies statistical models to predict future outcomes, \(Y\) based on a set of predictors, \(X\).32 Prediction models may be implemented using a wide range of approaches, including regression models, decision trees, and machine learning algorithms.31,32 The prediction models are fitted to data (the predictors) and the predicted output, \(Y´\) is evaluated based on the outcome, \(Y\).32 Evaluation metrics on prediction studies often include classification metrics such as area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity and calibration plots for binary outcomes33 and root mean square error (RMSE), for continuous outcomes.34

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.7 Machine Learning
The widespread adoption of CGM has generated large volumes of glucose data, enabling the application of machine learning methods in diabetes care.15,35 Machine learning is often associated with complex algorithms that are hard to interpret, however many machine learning methods are closely related to familiar statistical approaches.36 Similarly, linear regression can be applied in a data-driven modelling framework and are among the most interpretable machine learning methods.36 Machine learning models can in general be divided into supervised and unsupervised machine learning.36 Supervised machine learning uses labelled data where each sample (e.g., age and sex from one individual) has a label or an outcome (e.g., elevated NT-proBNP) to predict new outcomes for previously unseen data. Unsupervised machine learning on the other hand uses data without labels to explore underlying structures or clusters in data.36
Among supervised learning methods, deep neural networks are particularly notable because they can automatically extract information directly from raw data for tasks such as prediction or classification, reducing the need for manual feature engineering such as calculating CGM-derived metrics by hand.15,37 Consequently, deep neural networks offer an alternative to relying on predefined CGM-derived metrics. Since CGM data are collected continuously over time, methods that can account for temporal dependencies are particularly relevant. A long short-term memory model (LSTM) is a type of recurrent neural network, which have been designed for time-series data and used for glucose prediction tasks as illustrated in Figure 1.2.15,36,38 These models can use previous glucose values to inform predictions of future glucose levels, making them suitable for short-term forecasting.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.8 Foundation Models and Transfer Learning
In recent years, machine learning models have grown substantially in scale, complexity, and applicability. This development has led to the emergence of foundation models, which are defined as “any model that is trained on broad data (generally using self-supervision at scale) that can be adapted (e.g., fine-tuned) to a wide range of downstream tasks”.40 Two CGM specialized foundation models exist in the literature which both uses self-supervised machine learning.41,42 Self-supervised machine learning is a technique used to train models on unlabelled data through different techniques, one of them including masked learning (e.g., predicting manually masked words in text or values in time-series signals).40–42 A foundation model is first pretrained on a general task, such as predicting masked values in CGM data, allowing it to learn representations of glucose dynamics. These representations can subsequently be adapted to a downstream task, such as predicting cardiovascular outcomes, through transfer learning.40,42 A foundation model can be conceptualized as comprising a pretrained backbone and a task-specific head (Figure 1.3).43 The backbone extracts representations from the input data, whereas the head uses the representations to perform the downstream task. Transfer-learning strategies differ primarily in how the pretrained backbone is used. It may remain fixed and serve as a feature extractor, with only a downstream model or task-specific head being trained, or some or all of the model may be updated through fine-tuning.43,44 The choice of strategy depends partly on the similarity between the pretraining and downstream tasks.44 Transfer learning addresses the need for large amounts of data in deep neural networks by reusing knowledge learned from large datasets and applying it to related tasks with limited labelled data. This is particularly relevant in clinical risk prediction, where labelled data are often scarce, especially for minority populations.43,45,46

section: 1.9 Health Disparities and Bias in Machine Learning
text:
1.9 Health Disparities and Bias in Machine Learning
Fairness is being integrated more and more into reporting guidelines for clinical prediction models, because unequal model performance across population strata defined by sensitive attributes, such as race, sex, and socioeconomic status, may contribute to or reinforce societal inequalities.47,48 In clinical prediction modelling, fairness implies that models should perform accurately, equitably, and reliably across diverse populations. This requires transparent model development, evaluation, and monitoring, so that potential disparities can be identified and addressed.47 There is however still a lack of reporting on race and ethnicity in trials even though diabetes affects individuals across all racial and ethnic groups and differences have been reported in glycemic response, glycemic control, insulin resistance and the burden of diabetes-related complications between populations.54 A study by Turner et al.49 showed that among 20,692 US-based clinical trials, only 43% reported participants’ race or ethnicity. Although the reporting of race and ethnicity increased between 2010 and 2020, racial and ethnic minority groups remained underrepresented relative to their proportions in the US population.49 Furthermore, this lack of information is not only present in clinical trials but also in reportings of FDA-approved AI medical devices.46,49 A study by Muralidharan et al.46 found that only 3.6% of the FDA approval documents (Summary of Safety and Effectiveness Data Documents) provided information on race and/or ethnicity of the intended or testet users.46 Lack of ethnic and racial information in datasets problematic in data-driven models such as machine learning models since they reflect the populations represented in their training data and when minority groups are underrepresented, the resulting models may not generalize equally well to all patients.46,55 Consequently, models developed predominantly using one population may not achieve comparable predictive performance in others and potentially reinforcing existing healthcare disparities.55 For example, risk prediction models have been shown to underestimate the risk of T2D among non-Hispanic Black individuals,55 and algorithmic bias has been demonstrated to substantially influence the allocation of healthcare resources.56 Developing equitable prediction models therefore requires both representative data and careful evaluation of model performance across demographic groups. Transfer learning becomes particularly relevant in such cases where labelled data are often scarce, especially for minority populations.43,45,46,49

title: 2  Aims
text:
2.1 Overall Aim
Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) provides detailed information on glucose patterns that is not captured by HbA1c alone and may contribute to cardiovascular risk assessment. Machine learning offers opportunities to extract additional information directly from CGM time-series, but the predictive value and generalizability of these approaches remain uncertain. Moreover, models may perform differently across populations if demographic groups are inadequately represented in the training data. Evaluating the clinical potential of CGM data therefore requires consideration of predictive value, generalizability, and fairness. These knowledge gaps formed the basis for the aims of this dissertation.
The overall aim of this PhD dissertation was to investigate the potential of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data to improve cardiovascular risk assessment and to evaluate the role of machine learning in extracting clinically relevant information from CGM data across different diabetes populations, including the evaluation of racial disparities in model performance.

title: 2  Aims
text:
2.2 Specific Aims
Aim 1: To identify and summarize the existing literature on associations between glycemic control and cardiovascular outcomes, and the use of CGM-derived metrics for cardiovascular risk prediction. (Study I)
Aim 2: To determine whether a CGM foundation model learns meaningful glucose representations in individuals with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. (Study II)
Aim 3: To evaluate whether traditional CGM-derived metrics and learned glucose representations improve prediction of elevated NT-proBNP beyond established clinical risk factors in individuals with type 2 diabetes. (Study II)
Aim 4: To evaluate the fairness of machine learning models for glucose prediction by assessing model performance across non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White populations. (Study III)

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.1 Study I: Scoping Review Methodology
In this chapter the three studies included in this PhD are presented together with a description of the datasets and methods used in the studies.
A scoping review was conducted to investigate current knowledge of CGM-data and its possible connection and predictive power to clinical and subclinical cardiovascular outcomes. Given the expected heterogeneity between studies and the broad exploratory nature of the research question, a scoping review was considered the most appropriate methodology, as the aim was to map the existing evidence within this field.1 The scoping review followed the Manual for Evidence Synthesis (Chapter 10 - Scoping reviews) from the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyzes extension for scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines.1,2

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.1.1 Concepts and Definitions
The review focused exclusively on studies using CGM data as input for analyzes of associations with, or prediction of, cardiovascular disease (CVD). This meant that studies only investigating self-monitored blood glucose with finger-prick measurements or blood sample measurements such as HbA1c were not considered in this review. CVD outcomes were divided into subclinical or clinical. For the clinical CVD, the following outcomes were considered: cardiovascular mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, coronary artery disease, heart failure, stroke, and peripheral artery disease with synonymous terms included (e.g., ischemic heart diseases) and clinical events (e.g., undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery). Subclinical CVD was grouped into six subcategories: arterial stiffness, flow resistance, arterial wall thickness, arterial wall composition, cardiac and pulse-related measures, and arterial lumen. CVD outcomes did not include broader risk factors nonspecific to cardiovascular risk (e.g., age or sex). Eligibility criterias for the scoping review3 can be found in Table 3.2.



Table 3.2: Eligibility criteria for the scoping review (Study I).





Inclusion Criteria
Exclusion Criteria




Human clinical studies including participants with prediabetes or any type of diabetes except for gestational diabetes, regardless of definitions
Review articles, editorials, case reports, protocols, conference abstracts, and preprints.


Peer-reviewed published original articles (including brief reports).
Animal studies not including any human participants.


Studies investigating either:
Studies not including metrics derived from continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) device data


  a) The association between CGM-derived metrics of glycemic control and cardiovascular risk markers or cardiovascular diseases (prevalent or incident).
Studies including CGM-derived metrics as outcomes.


  b) CGM-derived metrics of glycemic control as predictors of cardiovascular risk markers or cardiovascular diseases (prevalent or incident).
Studies not focusing on CVD outcomes according to our definition, as outlined in Section 3.1.1.



Studies focusing on pregnant women with any form of diabetes including gestational diabetes.



Studies where participants were monitored post-surgery or during hospitalization (e.g., Intensive care unit).



Language not understood by authors








3.1.2 Search and Selection of Sources
MEDLINE and Embase were searched from inception to March 11, 2025. The two databases were selected because they are core databases for biomedical literature. The search was not extended to additional databases because of the resources available to the review team. The search strategy was developed in collaboration with information specialists. An exploratory search was conducted and 13 studies within the field was identified and used to test the search strategy with, by ensuring the 13 identified studies were included in the final search.4–16. The search strategy was wished to be kept broad as it was known beforehand that the field contained inconsistent terminology and overlapping search categories (e.g., ‘blood glucose monitoring’ and ‘glycemic control’ both encompass finger-prick measurements) in order to ensure identification of all the relevant studies in MEDLINE and Embase. The full search strategy can be found in Appendix A.
All identified records were uploaded into the software tool EPPI reviewer 6 and duplicates were removed.17 Titles and abstracts were screened by at least two independent reviewers and a meeting was held after ~5% of the titles and abstracts had been screened, to resolve disagreements and ensure consistency between reviewers. Afterwards full-text screening was performed by two independent reviewers and held up against eligibility criteria. Disagreements were resolved through discussion at physical meetings between reviewers.
Backward and forward citation searching was performed on all the included studies after the screening process using citationchaser18 and the screening process was repeated until no further new studies were identified through citationchaser.


3.1.3 Data Charting Process and Data Items
Research questions were defined before the screening process and data was extracted based on the research questions in Note 3.1.






Note 3.1: Research Questions (Study 1)




Is there an association between glycemic control and CVD risk?
Can CGM-derived metrics predict CVD risk?
What CGM-derived metrics are used in the literature?
Which cardiovascular markers and diseases are included as outcomes in the studies?
What characterizes study populations (age, sex, ethnicity, geographic location)?
What study designs are used (e.g., longitudinal cohort studies, randomized controlled trials, cross-sectional studies)?
How was data collected (e.g., clinical trial, epidemiological study, routinely collected data)?
What CGM devices were used?
What statistical models were used in the studies?
Is the data openly available?
Is the code openly available?





3.1.4 Synthesis of Results
Study characteristics were synthesized using descriptive statistics and supplemented by a narrative summary. Only the most adjusted models in the main population for each study was considered in this review. This approach was necessary as several studies reported numerous estimates across varying adjustments, different combinations of CGM-derived metrics and CVD outcomes, and/or distinct subgroup stratifications. Given the large volume of literature, studies investigating clinical cardiovascular outcomes were prioritized in the main synthesis. While subclinical markers offer valuable insight into early vascular changes and disease progression, clinical outcomes are more directly relevant to cardiovascular risk prediction and clinical decision-making. The main synthesis of clinical outcomes included both effect estimates and measures of statistical significance whereas the supplementary synthesis on subclinical CVD focused primarily on creating an overview of the chosen CGM-derived metrics and the statistical significance of reported associations. All evaluation metrics mentioned in the studies doing prediction analyzes were reported based on what the studies reported.

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.2 Datasets used in this dissertation
Two datasets were used in this PhD project and are described in the following sections. The datasets were obtained from studies that were conducted independently of this PhD project. Both studies were conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and were approved by the relevant institutional review boards or ethics committees. For the T1DX dataset, ethical approval is documented in Bergenstal et al.19 and for the CANCAN study, approval was obtained from the Committee on Health Research Ethics in the Central Denmark Region(#93931 and #1-10-72-221-21). Oral and written informed consent was obtained from all participants.

3.2.1 CANCAN Data
The CANCAN dataset was collected in an observational case-control study from two hospital outpatient clinics (Denmark). The aim of the CANCAN study was to investigate if cardiac autonomic neuropathy (CAN) assessments, CGM and heart failure indicators could be used in risk stratification for people with T2D. Participants were included if they were adults (> 18 years old) and had T2D for at least a year. Exclusion criteria were atrial fibrillation or laser-treated eye disease within the past three months, were pregnant or lactating, had a life-threatening disease (expected survival < 1 year), or had cognitive disabilities rendering them unable to understand and give consent. Data were collected during a clinical examination, during which blood samples to obtain NT-proBNP was collected together with urine samples, and a blinded CGM sensor was inserted.(Figure 3.1). In total, 159 participants were included since the rest were missing age, sex, HbA1c, BMI, NT-proBNP, HDL, total cholesterol, or eGFR, which were needed for the analyzes in Study II.






Figure 3.1: Data collection timeline for the CANCAN study.





3.2.2 T1D Exchange Data
The publicly available T1D Exchange (T1DX) dataset, distributed by the Jaeb Center for Health Research under the protocol “Racial Differences in Mean CGM Glucose in Relation to HbA1c”, was collected in 10 diabetes centers (US).20 The data was collected to determine if there is a racial difference in the association between mean glucose and HbA1c between non-Hispanic Black (Black) and non-Hispanic White (White) people with T1D. In the T1DX study ethnicity and race was defined through self-identified and self-reported ethnicity/race verification forms where ethnicity was defined as Hispanic or Latino as: “a person of Cuban, Mexican, Puerto Rican, South or Central American, or other Spanish culture or origin, regardless of race. The term “Spanish origin” could be used in addition to “Hispanic” or “Latino”“.19 in Supplementary Material For race a participant defined as White was “a person having origins in any of the original peoples of Europe, the Middle East or North Africa.” and Black or African American people were defined as “a person having origins in any of the Black racial groups of Africa. Terms such as “Haitian” or “Negro” can be used in addition to “Black” or “African American””.19 in Supplementary Material In this dissertation, the term race will be used moving forward, as it aligns with the terminology used by Bergenstal et al.19. However, I acknowledge that it is difficult to define race.21 Of the 205 participants included in the study19, 101 were White and 104 were Black. For each race, two age groups were sampled 8 to <18 years old and >18. Each participant wore a blinded modified investigational version of Abbott Diabetes Care’s Flash Glucose Monitoring System (CGM) as continuously as possible for 12 weeks (Figure 3.2). CGM data was sampled every 15 minutes in a range between 2.21 - 27.65 mmol/L (40 and 498 mg/dL). Blood samples were taken at enrollment, at some of the follow-up visits, and at the end of enrollment.






Figure 3.2: Data collection timeline for the T1DX study.

title: 3  Methods
section: 3.3 Study II: Foundation Models and Predictive Utility of CGM data
text:
3.3 Study II: Foundation Models and Predictive Utility of CGM data
The second study investigated whether a CGM foundation model could learn meaningful representations of CGM data and compared these learned representations with conventional CGM-derived metrics identified in Study I.3

3.3.1 Data and Participant Selection
Both the CANCAN and the T1DX dataset were used for Study II. Participants with missing age, sex, HbA1c or BMI were excluded from both cohorts and in addition, CANCAN participants with missing NT-proBNP, HDL, total cholesterol, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also removed, since those are necessary to calculate the SCORE2-Diabetes risk score with. T1DX participants with missing race data were also removed. Days with less than 70% of CGM data were removed in addition to participants with less than one day of data from both datasets to ensure sufficient data for the analyzes. Values exceeding the measurable range of the CGM devices were retained as the device’s upper and lower measurement limits. For the CANCAN data, this range was 2.2 - 27.8 mmol/L and for the T1DX data, the range was 2.21 - 27.65 mmol/L. 


3.3.2 Transfer Learning, Foundation Models and Embeddings
Of the two CGM-specific foundation models based on self-supervised learning currently described in the literature (CGMformer by Lu et al., 202522 and GLUformer by Lutsker et al., 202623), only the pretrained weights from the CGMformer were made publicly available, enabling reuse of the model for downstream tasks. The CGMformer was therefore chosen and the data was organized in 24-hour long-format input to match the input requirements of the CGMformer. The output of the foundation model is learned representations of the input data, also known as embeddings and the head of the CGMformer were not available for retraining (Figure 3.3). By only having the backbone, the transfer learning strategy being used had to be replacing the head with a new, as shown in Figure 1.3 as transfer three.






Figure 3.3: Illustration of how CGMformer is used in this analyzis.



The CGMformer gives a 128-dimensional embedding vector for each 24-hour CGM data input. Embeddings are numerical vectors that summarize the characteristics of the input glucose profile. A simple vector can be drawn as an arrow in a 2-dimensional and a 3-dimensional space as shown in Figure 3.4.













Figure 3.4: Embeddings shown as 2-dimensional and 3-dimensional vectors with the angle \(\theta\) between the two embeddings.



Because embeddings are numerical vectors, they can be compared to quantify the similarity between glucose profiles, as demonstrated by Lutsker et al.23 We therefore adopted a similar approach to assess the similarity between CGM-derived embeddings. Cosine similarity was calculated and it measures the angle between two embedding vectors independent of their magnitude (the length of the vectors). The cosine similarity is calculated by measuring the cosine angle between two vectors as shown by \(\theta\) in Figure 3.4. The cosine similarity is a number between -1 and 1, where 1 means the two vectors are identical, 0 means they are unrelated, and -1 means that they are pointing in opposite directions (Figure 3.5). For the analyzes in this study, cosine distance, calculated as 1 − cosine similarity, was used because it expresses similarity as a distance measure, allowing embeddings with similar orientations to have small distances and facilitating downstream analyzes and visualizations. The cosine distances range from 0 to 2 where 0 means the two vectors are pointing in the same direction, 1 means they are unrelated, and 2 means that they are pointing in opposite directions.






Figure 3.5: Embeddings shown with different cosine similarities. The cosine similarity is calculated as the cosine of the angle (\(\theta\)) between two embeddings.



Kernel density plots were used to visualize the distribution of cosine distances within specific clinical strata and across differing participants (Figure 3.6). Groupings were made based on days from the same participant (within-participant comparison), days from different participants with the same clinical strata (between-participant comparison), and days from different participants with different clinical strata (between-participant comparison) (Figure 3.6).






Figure 3.6: Glucose variability strata is used as an example to illustrate the cosine distance analyzis of the within and between cosine distance pairs.



The main focus for the participant comparisons were TIR and HbA1c. The thresholds were as followed: TIR ≥ 70% (70–180 mg/dL, 3.9–10.0 mmol/L) and HbA1c <7.0 % (< 53 mmol/mol).24,25 Furthermore, a uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) algorithm was used to reduce the dimensionality of the embeddings to two dimensions since a 128-dimensional vector is not easily visualized. UMAP visualizations were generated by coloring participants according to race, MAGE (< 70 mg/dL ( < 3.9 mmol/L )),24 and NT-proBNP (NT-proBNP ≤ 125 pg/mL).26,27 The threshold-based categorizations for TIR, MAGE, and HbA1c were used solely for the cosine distance analyzes and to facilitate interpretation of the UMAP visualizations and were not incorporated into model development or any statistical analyzes. The concept of dimensionality reduction is illustrated in Figure 3.7. The UMAPs were first used for visualization and comparison with existing literature and were subsequently included in prediction models.22,23,28 This dimensionality reduction step was used because the original 128-dimensional embeddings would provide too many predictors for a simple logistic regression model. The UMAPs were colored by TIR, and MAGE to investigate if the embeddings were able to capture relevant information about glycemic patterns. Elevated NT-proBNP for the CANCAN embeddings were also used to color the UMAPs to investigate if the embeddings were able to capture relevant information about cardiovascular risk and race was used to color the T1DX embeddings to investigate if the embeddings were able to capture relevant information about racial differences in glycemic patterns. Pearson correlations were calculated between the UMAP dimensions and HbA1c, TIR, MAGE, and log-transformed NT-proBNP.






Figure 3.7: Conceptual illustration of dimensionality reduction, read from left to right. High-dimensional information can be represented in fewer dimensions while preserving important structure, however not all information is retained. The illustration does not show how UMAP works specifically, but conveys the general idea of reducing complex data to a lower-dimensional representation.

title: 3  Methods
text:
3.4 Study II: Cardiovascular Risk Assessment
The following section describes the cardiovascular risk assessment analyzes, in which N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was predicted as a binary outcome using a >125 pg/mL threshold.26,27,29 Only the cross-sectional CANCAN dataset was used for the cardiovascular risk assessment. The focus was to test the predictive power of CGM data both as represented as embeddings and as well-established CGM-derived metrics. Some models also included clinical predictors to compare up against baseline models. Prediction models integrated clinical, standard CGM-derived, and learned representations.

3.4.1 Predictors
Initial testing showed that the numbers of predictors had to be limited due to the small sample size and the SCORE2-Diabetes risk score was chosen as another way to represent the clinical predictor set while keeping the number of predictors down.30 This resulted in the following clinical predictors: age, sex, smoking status, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL cholesterol), age at diabetes diagnosis, eGFR and HbA1c. The SCORE2-Diabetes risk score was tested as a predictor in itself as well. Additionally, age was tested as a predictor on its own to see if it was a strong predictor of elevated NT-proBNP, since NT-proBNP is known to increase with age.29,31 TIR and MAGE were chosen as they were the CGM-derived metrics most commonly used in the literature based on the findings from Study I.3 All CGM-derived metrics in this dissertationwere calculated using the Interpreting Glucose Data from Continuous Glucose Monitors (IGLU) package32,33 in R (default settings). TIR was calculated as the percentage of time spent in the range of 3.9–10.0 mmol/L (70–180 mg/dL).24 MAGE was calculated as the mean amplitude of glucose excursions, where the included excursions were consecutive peak-to-nadir (or nadir-to-peak) glucose differences exceeding one standard deviation of the individual’s glucose measurements. The IGLU implementation computationally reproduces the original manual procedure proposed by Service et al.34 The CGMformer generated one 128-dimensional embedding for each 24-hour CGM recording. Because NT-proBNP was measured at the participant level, a single embedding was required for each participant. Therefore, embeddings from multiple recording days were aggregated using pooling to obtain one participant-level embedding. Both minimum, maximum, and mean pooling were explored to determine the most effective aggregation method. Maximum pooling was considered the default based on existing literature.23 The resulting 128-dimensional embeddings were subsequently reduced to two dimensions using UMAP, thereby enabling their use in the prediction models while minimising the number of predictors.


3.4.2 Model Development and Evaluation
Prediction models were developed using logistic regression to predict elevated NT-proBNP (>125 pg/mL) as a binary outcome. The models were evaluated using the AUROC as the primary metric. Bootstrap with optimism correction was employed for internal validation because of the limited sample size and the absence of an external validation cohort.35–37 The method repeatedly sampled bootstrap samples by sampling with replacement from the original dataset (Figure 3.8). Sampling with replacement means that the same observation can be selected more than once in the new sample. For each bootstrap sample, the prediction model is fitted and its performance is evaluated both in the bootstrap sample (apparent performance) and in the original dataset (test performance). The difference between these two performance estimates represents the optimism due to overfitting (overfitting occurs when a model learns overly specific patterns in the training data, causing it to perform well on training data but poorly on new data). Averaging the optimism across all bootstrap samples and subtracting it from the apparent performance of the model fitted to the full dataset yields an optimism-corrected estimate of model performance. Internal validation was performed using 500 bootstrap resamples.35,37 Prediction stability plots were reported for each model to evaluate the stability of predictions produced by a specific model strategy when the training data changes.37

section: 3.5 Study III: Algorithmic Fairness and Blood Glucose Prediction

3.5 Study III: Algorithmic Fairness and Blood Glucose Prediction
The third study investigated racial bias strictly based on blood glucose measurements from a CGM device. Although the primary focus of this dissertationis cardiovascular risk assessment, glucose forecasting provides an appropriate setting for investigating algorithmic fairness in CGM-based machine learning. In contrast to participant-level cardiovascular prediction, glucose forecasting is trained on a continuous stream of CGM measurements, allowing each participant to contribute numerous samples over the recording period rather than a single outcome. This results in substantially more training examples, enabling the development and evaluation of more complex machine learning models. Consequently, glucose forecasting provides a suitable framework for studying how training data composition influences model performance across racial groups.

3.5.1 Preprocessing of CGM data for Forecasting
A prediction horizon of 60 minutes was chosen as it provides sufficient time for preventive interventions for hypo- and hyperglycemia, such as insulin dose adjustments or carbohydrate intake, while accounting for the 15-minute sampling interval of the CGM device and the physiological delay between blood and interstitial glucose measurements.25 Accordingly, the CGM data was divided into consecutive 60-minute windows containing four glucose measurements to predict glucose levels 60 minutes into the future, as illustrated in Figure 3.9. Prediction windows containing missing CGM values were excluded.






Figure 3.9: The prediction horizon and overview of the creation of samples (predictors and outcomes).





3.5.2 Partitioning of the Dataset
The T1DX dataset was randomly resampled without replacement at the participant level to avoid data leakage and to evaluate model performance on independent participants. As illustrated in Figure 3.10, training subsets with varying proportions of Black and White participants were generated by randomly selecting participants from the original dataset while keeping the train-test split at the participant level. Eleven training set compositions were created, ranging from 100% White and 0% Black to 0% White and 100% Black participants in 10% increments.
Because some training subsets consisted entirely of participants from a single racial group, the maximum training set size on participant level was constrained by the size of the smaller racial group minus the participants kept for testing. Consequently, each training subset contained approximately half the number of participants in the original T1DX dataset. Repeating this procedure for each participant resulted in 2,255 training datasets (205 participants × 11 training set compositions) and 205 independent test sets. Throughout all resampling procedures, all CGM recordings from a participant were kept together to prevent data leakage between the training and test sets.






Figure 3.10: The prediction horizon and overview of the creation of subsets for training.



Eleven subsets were created for each of the participants and the last week’s data was chosen to test on as illustrated in Figure 3.11. To preserve sample size, one week was chosen because participants had varying amount of CGM data and the participant with the least amount of data had ~ 2 weeks. The remaining data was used for training the models.






Figure 3.11: The splitting of a participants data to create training and test sets.





3.5.3 Model Selection and Training Approaches
A long short-term memory model (LSTM) network architecture based on van Doorn et al.38 was used (two LSTM layers followed by a dense layer). All the training data was scaled to be within the range of zero to one. Hyperparameters were optimized once prior to the repeated model development using grid search and data from all participants except the last week. The gridsearch included the number of neurons in the LSTM layers, activation function, dropout rate, batch size, learning rate, learning rate decay, and early stopping patience. The selected hyperparameter configuration was subsequently fixed and applied to all LSTM models. The complete hyperparameter tuning procedure and implementation are available in the accompanying GitHub repository.39 Four training approaches were used when the models for each participant were developed as described below and illustrated in Figure 3.12.
Additionally, Three LSTM models and the last observation carried forward (LOCF) as a naive baseline.

LOCF: In the LOCF model, a given CGM measurement (x4) was used to predict blood glucose values 60 minutes in advance (x8) in the test set by assuming no change in the last 60 minutes.
Base-Individual: In the Base-Individual model, each participant’s complete CGM data (except for the last week, which was used for the testing data) was used for training.
Base-Generalized: Here, for each participant, the 11 corresponding training datasets described above were used to generate 11 separate models, which were all subsequently tested on the given participant’s last week of CGM data.
Transfer Learned: This model mirrored the Base-Generalized Model’s setup. However, the 11 trained models for each participant were subsequently tailored to the given participant’s complete CGM data (except for the last week, which was used for the testing data). The transfer learning technique used is described as transfer 2 in Figure 1.3.







Figure 3.12: The four training approaches. The Base-Individual, Base-Generalized, and Transfer Learned models were based on an LSTM architecture. The base layer (green) consisted of two LSTM layers, while the task-specific layer (blue) consisted of a single dense layer. Abbreviation: LOCF, last observation carried forward.





3.5.4 Model Evaluation
To evaluate model performance, each participant’s last week’s data (672 measurements) was reserved for internal testing (Figure 3.11). Model accuracy was assessed by calculating the root mean squared error (RMSE) for each participant across all four modeling approaches. For the LOCF and Base-Individual models, this yielded one RMSE value for each of the 101 White participants and 104 Black participants. For the Base-Generalized and Transfer Learned models, RMSE values were calculated for each participant across 11 data subsets, each representing a unique proportion of White and Black participants. Performance was summarized as the mean RMSE with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for each racial group. It was further assumed that the varying proportions of Black and White participants in the training data subsets would affect the performance and an interaction term was therefore added. The interaction term allowed for different slopes in the LMEM which allowed us to test the hypotheses. It was hypothesized that when plotting the proportion of White participants in the training data against the RMSE, the slope would be negative for White participants and positive for Black participants (Figure 3.13). This would indicate that as the proportion of White participants in the training data increased, the RMSE decreased for White participants and increased for Black participants, indicating racial bias in the model. The Base-Individual model would perform the worst since it was trained on the least amount of data and the Transfer Learned model would remove the slopes that were expected to be seen in the Base-Generalized models.






Figure 3.13: The hypotheses for the results of the linear mixed effect models.



Surveillance error grids (SEG) were used to get a general idea of the clinical risk of the prediction models.40 The error grids are originally developed for the regulatory bodies to asses clinical accuracy of blood glucose monitoring in post-surveillance before the wide spread use of CGM devices.40,41 and the results should therefore be interpreted with caution when using CGM data. The SEG is a 600x600 grid assigned an individual risk score to each datapoint with 15 colored zones, each indicating severity of a monitoring error that is acted upon in regards to risk of hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia (Figure 3.14).41 To facilitate interpretation, the 15 surveillance error grid zones were collapsed into the five broader risk zones (“No”, “Slight”, “Moderate”, “High”, and “Extreme”), as previously suggested in the literature.40 Predictions outside of 0–33 mmol/L were changed to 0 or 33 mmol/L to keep within the upper and lower bounds of the surveillance error grid.

4.1 Study I: Scoping Review Results
The study selection process is summarized in Figure 4.1. The MEDLINE and Embase search resulted in 4884 records screened on title and abstract, and 81 reports were assessed for eligibility based on full-text review by two independent reviewers. The citation search on the included 51 reports identified 2 additional reports, which finally resulted in 53 included reports in total. All included and excluded reports are reported in Appendix B.

4.1.1 Study Populations
The study population most common was people with T2D (34 of studies), then people with T1D (20 of 53) and lastly prediabetes (4 of 53). Most studies included adult participants, whereas seven focused on children younger than 18 years. Two studies included only male participants, whereas the remaining studies included both male and female participants.
The geographic distribution was found based on the hospitals and centers where data was collected or by the first author’s affiliation when the other options were not available. The distribution was uneven as shown in Figure 4.2. Most studies were conducted in Asia (27 of 53) or Europe (22 of 53). Three studies included data from North America, one was conducted in Australia, and only one included data from an African country, although its study population was predominantly White.2 No data was included from South America (Appendix C).






Figure 4.2: Geographical location of the studies. Countries colored in red indicate the geographical locations where the studies were conducted. Figure was created using MapChart https://www.mapchart.net/.





4.1.2 Study Designs and Demographics
Only one study was a randomized controlled trial,3 and the remaining studies were observational. Most studies used a cross-sectional design, with the cardiovascular outcome assessed at the same time as the CGM sensor was given. Only six studies performed longitudinal analyzes. Study sample sizes varied considerably, ranging from 174 to 6,2255 participants, with a median of 152. CGM data were obtained either from participants’ own devices (11 studies) or from CGM devices provided as part of the study (42 studies). Statistical analyzes most commonly included linear regression (22 studies) and logistic regression (22 studies), followed by Spearman or Pearson correlation analyzes (11 studies) and Cox proportional hazards regression (3 studies). Several studies performed additional exploratory analyzes, such as correlation analyzes, to identify relevant covariates for inclusion in regression models.
All included studies primarily investigated associations between CGM-derived measures and cardiovascular outcomes. Only three studies reported predictive performance measures as part of secondary analyzes,6–8 and none applied machine learning methods. Furthermore, none of the included studies provided openly available data or source code. Instead, availability was either not addressed or limited to access upon reasonable request from the corresponding author.


4.1.3 Continuous Glucose Monitoring
Medtronic CGM devices were the most frequently used (28 of 53 studies), followed by Abbott (9 of 53) and Dexcom (5 of 53). Other manufacturers included Menarini, Meiqi Company, and SIBIONICS. Sampling intervals ranged from 3 to 15 minutes but were reported in only a minority of studies (21 of 53). TIR (22 studies) and MAGE (23 studies) were the most frequently investigated CGM-derived metrics (Table 4.1). When stratified by T1D and T2D then TIR was the most frequently investigated metric in T1D populations (10 of 23 studies), whereas MAGE was less commonly investigated (5 of 22 studies). In T2D populations, TIR and MAGE were investigated in 11 of 23 and 14 of 22 studies, respectively. Studies conducted in T2D populations also tended to include larger sample sizes than those in T1D populations (median [IQR]: TIR, 510 [405–600] vs. 214 [119–547]; MAGE, 251 [89–411] vs. 57 [30–215]).

Only three studies evaluated the predictive performance of CGM-derived metrics for cardiovascular outcomes, all using logistic regression models with MAGE as the predictor. An overview of the most frequently used CGM-derived metrics stratified based on clinical and subclinical cardiovascular outcomes are shown in Table 4.4. Outcomes related to subclinical cardiovascular outcomes were more frequently studied (59 studies) compared to clinical outcomes (26 studies) and studies were predominantly done among people with T2D. Among clinical cardiovascular outcomes, coronary artery disease was examined most frequently (6 studies), followed by macrovascular complications (5 studies) and the Gensini score (4 studies) and for subclinical cardiovascular outcomes, particularly arterial wall thickness were frequently investigated (19 studies), arterial stiffness (12 studies), cardiac and pulse-related measures (10 studies), and flow resistance (9 studies).
TIR was the most commonly reported CGM-derived metric across most arterial-stiffness outcomes, followed by MAGE, MBG, SD, and CV. title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.1 Study I: Evidence for CGM in Cardiovascular Risk Assessment
The overall aim of this dissertation was to investigate the potential of CGM data and machine learning methods for cardiovascular risk assessment. To address this aim, the dissertation combined a systematic evaluation of the existing literature with the assessment of learned representations from a foundation model and an investigation of algorithmic fairness in glucose prediction. The following discussion integrates the findings of these three studies, and considers their methods and results in relation to existing literature.
Through the literature 53 studies investigating the link between CGM-data and CVD outcomes were identified. There were very inconsistent findings across the literature. A wide range of CGM-derived metrics were investigated in relation to both clinical and subclinical cardiovascular outcomes, and the statistical adjustment strategies varied considerably between studies. It was observed that studies focusing on people with T2D had bigger study populations and more consistently found evidence for associations compared to studies focusing on people with T1D which may indicate a lack of statistical power in the studies with T1D, which may explain some of the inconsistencies across the studies uncovered in the scoping review. The current evidence base is also limited by its geographical concentration mainly in Asia and Europe and by its almost exclusive focus on association analyzes. Only three studies evaluated the predictive value of MAGE, indicating that its potential for cardiovascular risk prediction remains insufficiently investigated.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.1.1 TIR, MAGE and Cardiovascular Outcomes
TIR was the most frequently investigated CGM-derived metric, particularly for clinical CVD outcomes, although associations were inconsistent across studies, as also reported in a previous review.1 The second most frequently investigated CGM-derived metric was MAGE. It seemed more consistently associated with coronary artery disease and severity scores, despite the smaller sample size compared to TIR however this is strictly based on a small section of the included studies. Furthermore, MAGE was the only CGM-derived metric evaluated for its predictive performance, and this was limited to coronary artery disease and subclinical peripheral artery disease. Although MAGE outperformed HbA1c as a predictor in these studies,2,3 the prediction models demonstrated only modest discriminative ability. This may indicate that within-day glucose variability is a relevant cardiovascular risk factor. However, MAGE is not a complete measure of glucose variability and is biased toward detecting hyperglycemic excursions.4 Consequently, MAGE may underestimate the contribution of hypoglycemia to cardiovascular risk. However, the literature remains inconclusive regarding the relative importance of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia in relation to cardiovascular outcomes. Some studies have reported associations between hyperglycemia-focused CGM-derived metrics and cardiovascular outcomes,3,5 others have reported associations between hypoglycemia-related CGM-derived metrics and cardiovascular outcomes,6–11 with some concluding that hypoglycemic excursions are associated with macrovascular complications, whereas hyperglycemic excursions are associated with microvascular complications.6,10 Together, these findings suggest that although within-day glucose variability may be an important cardiovascular risk factor, both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia may contribute to cardiovascular risk and should be considered when evaluating CGM-derived metrics.


5.1.2 Study Designs
Another component contributing to the heterogeneity were the difference in how the statistical analyzes were performed across studies. CGM-derived metrics were defined over different time periods or split up into ranges and thresholds were changed for TIR, time below range (TBR) and time above range (TAR) across different studies. Adjustment strategies varied substantially between studies, reflecting differences in study objectives and analytical approaches. The covariates varied between studies even though most studies adjusted for established cardiovascular risk factors, particularly demographic characteristics, medical history, biochemical variables, and anthropometric measures, limiting direct comparability of the reported associations. Only a minority of studies adjusted for additional CGM-derived metrics. Whether such adjustment is appropriate depends on the research question, as many CGM-derived metrics capture overlapping aspects of glycemic control. Furthermore, no substantial differences were observed between unadjusted and the most extensively adjusted estimates, suggesting that adjustment for additional covariates generally had only a modest influence on the reported associations.
The heterogeneity of the literature and the challenges of describing glucose variability through CGM-derived metrics provided part of the rationale for evaluating foundation model-derived representations in the subsequent study, as the complete CGM time-series can be used directly without first reducing it to manually engineered CGM-derived metrics. As a result, information on hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, mean glucose, glucose variability within and between days, and temporal glucose patterns can all be incorporated simultaneously.

title: 5  Discussion
section: 5.2 Study II: Learning Meaningful Representations from CGM data
text:
5.2 Study II: Learning Meaningful Representations from CGM data

Study II showed that CGMformer, the foundation model developed by Lu et al.,12 captured both long- and short-term glucose fluctuations, as assessed using traditional CGM-derived metrics, in individuals with T1D and T2D. However, the learned representations (embeddings) did not show clear patterns when stratified by CVD-related variables or race. Nevertheless, these findings suggest that CGMformer can generalize beyond its original training population of Chinese individuals with normal glucose tolerance, impaired glucose regulation, and T2D, because it captured clinically meaningful glycemic patterns in both the Danish CANCAN cohort of people with advanced T2D and the US T1DX cohort of people with T1D.
In Study II, cosine distances were lower within-participants than between-participants, indicating that the CGM embeddings captured participant-specific patterns. Similar findings have been reported by Lu et al,12 who observed higher within-participant cosine similarity (1-cosine distance), and by Lutsker et al.,13 who found lower within-participant cosine distances using the GLUFormer foundation model trained on an Israeli cohort from the Human Phenotype Project.14 Collectively, these findings support that CGM foundation models learn stable, individualized representations of glucose dynamics while also capturing common glycemic characteristics shared among individuals with similar glucose control as well as generalize across independent populations and diabetes types. By learning directly from the complete CGM time-series, these representations provide an alternative to manually engineered CGM-derived metrics and establish a reusable foundation for downstream clinical applications. Similar transitions from manually extracted metrics to learned representations have driven performance improvements in fields such as computer vision and natural language processing, where pretrained foundation models have become the standard approach for downstream prediction tasks.15 Whether these learned representations translate into improved predictive performance was subsequently investigated in Study II.

title: 5  Discussion
section: 5.3 Study II: Incremental Value of CGM-derived Information for NT-proBNP Prediction
text:
5.3 Study II: Incremental Value of CGM-derived Information for NT-proBNP Prediction
Although previous studies12,13 have successfully used foundation models to predict CVD-related outcomes, the learned representations in the Study II did not improve prediction of elevated NT-proBNP beyond established clinical predictors and were associated with increased model complexity. The optimism-corrected performance estimates indicate that the more complex models were susceptible to overfitting, reinforcing the conclusion that the learned representations did not provide robust improvements beyond established clinical predictors. This does not necessarily indicate that foundation model-derived representations are unsuitable for cardiovascular prediction. Rather, their performance may depend on the downstream modeling strategy. In Study II, the embeddings were incorporated as fixed predictors in logistic regression models, whereas Lu et al.12 fine-tuned (Figure 1.3, Transfer 1) the CGMformer and achieved an AUROC above 0.70 for predicting macrovascular complications. Similarly, Lutsker et al.13 demonstrated that a GLUFormer-derived risk score outperformed HbA1c in stratifying individuals according to cardiovascular-related mortality risk. However, the limited sample size and the lack of datasets containing both CGM data and cardiovascular outcomes precluded the use of more complex downstream models and task-specific fine-tuning as performed in Lu et al.12 and Lutsker et al.13 Furthermore, reducing the embeddings to UMAP dimensions in Study II may have resulted in the loss of predictive information, which could partly explain the limited performance of the prediction models. The different findings may also reflect differences in the predicted outcomes. Whereas previous studies predicted clinical cardiovascular events or mortality, Study II focused on elevated NT-proBNP, a biomarker that is affected by cardiac dysfunction in addition to non-cardiac factors such as age and renal function.16,17 Consequently, glucose-derived embeddings may have a weaker relationship with NT-proBNP than with clinical cardiovascular outcomes although this remains speculative. Together, these findings suggest that the successful application of foundation model representations to complex clinical outcomes may depend on the downstream modelling strategy and subsequently having access to substantially larger datasets than what was available in Study II.

5.3.1 Learned representations as predictors
While learned representations did not translate into improved prediction of elevated NT-proBNP, TIR and MAGE as standalone predictors did. In Study II, when adding TIR and MAGE to the clinical prediction model resulted in a higher optimism-corrected AUROC compared with the model based on clinical variables alone. However, the performance of these models was also considered relative to a simpler benchmark model based on age alone. The simpler baseline model showed substantial predictive ability, consistent with the well-established association between increasing age and NT-proBNP concentrations in both healthy populations and individuals with T2D.18 Together, these findings suggest that although readily available clinical variables capture much of the information relevant for predicting elevated NT-proBNP, CGM-data may still provide information that could contribute to future cardiovascular risk assessment.


5.3.2 CGM-derived metrics and CVD
Traditional CGM-derived metrics remain highly relevant for clinical prediction. Metrics such as TIR quantify well-established aspects of glycemic control, are readily understood by clinicians, and are already incorporated into routine diabetes management. Their simplicity and established clinical interpretation make them useful reference measures when assessing whether more complex learned representations provide additional predictive information. Previous studies have similarly demonstrated prognostic value for MAGE in individuals with acute coronary syndrome19,20, and greater glucose variability has been associated with higher NT-proBNP concentrations in this population20. Participants with elevated NT-proBNP in the CANCAN cohort exhibited characteristics consistent with more advanced disease but also had lower BMI and more favorable glycemic profiles. Although these findings may appear counterintuitive, lower BMI has previously been associated with poorer outcomes in patients with established heart failure, while obesity is associated with lower circulating NT-proBNP concentrations21. Overall, these findings further illustrates the complex relationship between glycemic control, body composition, and cardiovascular.

title: 5  Discussion
section: 5.4 Study III: Fairness of CGM-based Machine Learning Models
text:
5.4 Study III: Fairness of CGM-based Machine Learning Models
While Studies I and II focused on whether learned representations and traditional CGM-derived metrics improved cardiovascular risk prediction, the final aim of the dissertation considered another important aspect of clinical prediction models: whether their performance is equitable across population subgroups.
Study III demonstrated that the racial composition of the training data influenced glucose-forecasting performance across racial groups. Although the observed differences were statistically significant, their magnitude was small and unlikely to be clinically meaningful. These differences were no longer evident after transfer learning, suggesting that adapting models to participant-specific data may reduce performance disparities associated with imbalanced training data. Overall, although training-data composition had only a limited effect on glucose prediction performance in this study, its potential influence should still be assessed when developing and evaluating machine-learning models for clinical use.
Previous studies have demonstrated the potential of transfer learning to improve model performance across various healthcare applications. In multi-ethnic cancer-omics datasets, transfer learning reduced performance disparities, suggesting that it may help mitigate some consequences of imbalanced training data.22 Benefits have also been reported in personalized glucose forecasting, where transfer learning improved performance across several prediction tasks.23,24 Overall, the present findings are largely consistent with the existing literature, as the transfer learned models achieved the best overall performance while also reducing the performance differences observed between racial groups.

title: 5  Discussion
text:
5.5 Methodological Considerations
The following section discusses methodological considerations related to the studies included in this dissertation. Particular attention is given to the use of previously collected datasets, the processing and representation of CGM data, model evaluation, dimensionality reduction, and fairness assessment. These considerations provide important context for interpreting the findings and for understanding the strengths and limitations of the methods applied throughout the dissertation.

5.5.1 Study I: The Scoping Review
Study I was a comprehensive mapping of the literature and to the best of my knowledge, identified more relevant studies than any previous review on the topic together with differentiation between association and prediction studies.1,25 The study found methodological heterogeneity, which limited the feasibility of synthesizing effect estimates consistently across studies. The findings were therefore presented descriptively by mapping the number of studies investigating different CGM-derived metrics and cardiovascular outcomes. Although this approach provides an overview of the scope and distribution of the existing evidence, it does not allow definitive conclusions to be drawn about the strength or consistency of associations between specific CGM-derived metrics and cardiovascular outcomes. Furthermore, the predominance of cross-sectional studies found in the scoping review limited the clinical interpretation of the evidence identified. Without temporal separation between CGM exposure and cardiovascular outcomes, it is unclear whether the observed glucose patterns preceded cardiovascular disease or resulted from the disease itself, associated behavioural changes, or intensified treatment. Reverse causality could therefore either produce apparent associations that emerged only after the development of CVD or reduce measurable pre-existing associations through subsequent treatment and behavioural changes. Lastly, only searching two databases might have led to missing relevant studies in other databases, however MEDLINE and Embase were deemed the most relevant biomedical databases and a broad search strategy was prioritized over searching other databases due to the mixed terminology in both CGM-derived metrics and cardiovascular outcomes.


5.5.2 Study II: The CGMformer and Cosine Distances
By externally evaluating CGMformer, developed by Lu et al.,12 Study II contributes to the validation of existing models, as recommended by Efthimiou et al.26 and provides evidence regarding the foundation model’s generalizability. For the evaluation of the foundation model, by combining comparisons with established CGM-derived metrics, cosine-distance analyzes, and visualizations, the study assessed both whether the representations captured clinically interpretable glycemic patterns and participant-specific glycemic characteristics. This provided greater insight into the content and potential utility of the learned representations. A limitation of the cosine-distance analyzes was the complex dependence structure of the observations. Participants contributed multiple days of CGM data and could therefore be represented in multiple distance comparisons. Consequently, the observations were not independent, making a conventional Mann–Whitney U test inappropriate. Statistical significance would also be difficult to interpret because treating all pairwise distances as independent would overstate the effective sample size and could produce misleadingly small \(p\)-values. In addition, the very large number of participant pairs would make even small differences statistically significant, further limiting the interpretability of conventional \(p\)-values. The cosine-distance results were therefore evaluated descriptively and visually, enabling exploration of potential group differences but not formal statistical inference.


5.5.3 Study II: Prediction of NT-proBNP
The use of bootstrapping with optimism correction allowed for robust internal validation, thereby reducing the risk of overfitting and overestimating the results which are important factors to take into consideration when working with limited real-world data. The relatively small sample size restricted the analyzes because the available data was deemed insufficient for task-specific fine-tuning of CGMformer, and the embeddings were instead incorporated as fixed predictors in comparatively simple downstream models. Reducing the embeddings to UMAP dimensions made the number of predictors manageable relative to the sample size but may have discarded information relevant to NT-proBNP. Consequently, the available data did not permit evaluation of the embeddings under task-specific fine-tuning, and their potential prognostic value therefore remains undetermined. Furthermore, dichotomizing NT-proBNP at 125 pg/mL may be an imperfect replacement for cardiovascular risk and heart failure, limiting the extent to which the analyzis could assess the relationship between CGM-derived representations and clinical cardiovascular outcomes. A more definitive evaluation would require substantially larger longitudinal datasets containing temporally aligned CGM measurements, relevant clinical covariates, and subsequent cardiovascular outcomes. However, such datasets remain rare, therefore limiting opportunities for task-specific fine-tuning or the development of more complex prediction models. Access to these data would enable assessment of whether the embeddings provide prognostic information beyond established cardiovascular risk factors and traditional CGM-derived metrics.


5.5.4 Study III: Fairness in Clinical Prediction Models
A key strength of Study III is its systematic evaluation of how the racial composition of training data influences predictive performance across groups. By examining multiple training strategies and varying group representation in the training data, the study provides a framework that could in addition be applied to fairness evaluations involving other populations, outcomes, and data modalities. The use of openly available data, together with publicly shared analytical code, further enhances the transparency and reproducibility of the study and facilitates extension of the approach in future research. However, the study included only non-Hispanic White and Black participants from the United States. Future studies should evaluate potential disparities across additional racial and ethnic groups and in other geographical settings. Fairness evaluations could also consider other demographic characteristics, such as age, given that glycemic control varies across the lifespan.27 Although algorithmic fairness is most commonly evaluated for binary classification using evaluation metrics such as demographic parity and equalized odds,28 comparable approaches for prediction of continuous outcomes remain less developed. Study III therefore provides a novel framework for evaluating disparities in glucose forecasting. However, the analyzis was computationally intensive even though only a shallow neural network was evaluated, because models were repeatedly trained across multiple racial compositions and training strategies for each participant. The computational requirements may therefore limit the feasibility of applying this framework to more complex models without access to considerable computing resources. The findings may also depend on the selected prediction horizon. Although a 60-minute horizon was chosen to allow time for potential preventive action, shorter forecasting horizons generally yield greater predictive accuracy. Future studies should determine whether the observed effects of racial composition and transfer learning are consistent across prediction horizons. In addition, the framework was evaluated using only a single US dataset and was not replicated in an independent cohort. Because the forecasting models were trained separately for each participant, external validation of the fitted models themselves was not directly applicable.
