title: 6  Conclusion
text:
This dissertation investigated the potential of CGM data and machine learning methods to improve cardiovascular risk assessment. Overall, the findings demonstrate both the opportunities and current limitations of using CGM data for this purpose. Although previous studies have reported associations between CGM-derived metrics and cardiovascular outcomes, the additional predictive value of traditional CGM-derived metrics and learned representations beyond established clinical predictors was limited in the present work. The dissertation further showed that foundation model-derived representations capture meaningful glycemic patterns and highlighted the importance of evaluating machine learning models across demographic groups. Together, these findings suggest that CGM may have a future role in cardiovascular risk prediction, but larger prospective studies are needed to determine whether both traditionally CGM-derived metrics and more complex methods to extract information from CGM data can meaningfully improve cardiovascular risk stratification in clinical practice.
These conclusions are supported by the findings corresponding to the four specific aims.
Aim 1: The scoping review identified a heterogeneous evidence base characterized by numerous studies of associations between glycemic control and cardiovascular outcomes but few studies evaluating the predictive value of CGM-derived metrics.
Aim 2: The external evaluation of CGMformer showed that its representations captured meaningful glycemic and participant-specific patterns in individuals with T1D and T2D, providing evidence of generalizability beyond the population in which the model was developed on.
Aim 3: Traditional CGM-derived metrics and learned representations from the foundation model provided limited additional value for identifying elevated NT-proBNP beyond established clinical predictors in individuals with T2D.
Aim 4: Glucose-forecasting performance differed between non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White participants. These disparities were influenced by the racial composition of the training data and the modelling strategy, while transfer learning showed potential as an approach for reducing some performance differences.

title: 7  Future perspectives
text:
7.1 CGM in future Cardiovascular Risk Prediction
The findings of this thesis do not currently support direct changes to clinical practice but identify several directions for future research.
Foundation models trained on CGM data may eventually enable more comprehensive use of glucose dynamics for cardiovascular risk assessment than traditional CGM-derived metrics. As machine learning methods continue to advance, alongside rapid developments in continuous glucose monitoring and automated insulin delivery technologies, the potential clinical value of CGM-derived information is likely to increase. This is particularly relevant given the increasing global prevalence of diabetes and its associated cardiovascular burden.
Although traditional CGM-derived metrics provided some predictive value for elevated NT-proBNP, age alone performed similarly while being substantially easier, less expensive, and non-invasive to obtain. Consequently, the additional clinical value of CGM-derived information must outweigh the increased burden and cost associated with collecting CGM data. However, for individuals who already use CGM as part of routine diabetes management, glucose-derived information may provide complementary insights into cardiovascular risk without requiring additional data collection. Unlike age, CGM-derived metrics reflect an individual’s temporal glucose variability, which may capture aspects of metabolic health that are potentially modifiable.

title: 7  Future perspectives
section: 7.2 Future Research on CGM Data and Prediction of Cardiovascular Outcomes
text:
7.2 Future Research on CGM Data and Prediction of Cardiovascular Outcomes
The potential relevance of CGM data for cardiovascular risk assessment is increasingly recognized, as reflected by the ongoing longitudinal FACULTY study, which includes approximately 70,000 participants using CGM devices.1 This study may provide an important opportunity to determine whether CGM-derived information adds prognostic value beyond established clinical predictors. However, studies of this scale are not always feasible, and progress in the field will also depend on the ability to synthesize evidence across smaller studies. In this regard, the heterogeneity identified in Study I highlights the need for greater methodological consistency. Wider adherence to consensus recommendations,2 could promote more consistent calculation and reporting of CGM-derived metrics. This should be accompanied by prespecified approaches to covariate adjustment, harmonized definitions of cardiovascular outcomes, and transparent documentation of analytical decisions. Greater consistency across these areas would facilitate meaningful comparisons between studies and provide a stronger basis for future systematic reviews and meta-analyzes.
In addition to methodological alignment, greater use of routinely collected CGM data could support larger and more cost-efficient studies that more closely reflect populations currently using CGM devices. Study I demonstrated that such data remain underused in research on cardiovascular complications. This may partly reflect restricted access to proprietary manufacturer platforms and difficulties linking CGM measurements with individual-level clinical records. In other fields, including medical image analyzis, progress has been accelerated by large, publicly available datasets.3–5 However, no equivalent resource currently combines CGM time series with information on diabetes-related complications although efforts have been made to gather an overview of publicly available datasets containing CGM data.6–8 Developing shared research resources or making existing databases more findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable in accordance with the FAIR principles could support reproducible research and accelerate progress in this field.9
Greater availability of large, well-characterized datasets would also make it more feasible to train and fine-tune CGM foundation models for cardiovascular applications. In particular, multimodal models could integrate CGM time series with established cardiovascular risk factors, laboratory measurements, treatment information, and data from other wearable devices. This may allow models to capture complementary information across data sources rather than relying solely on predefined CGM-derived metrics. Shared datasets would further enable standardized benchmarking and independent external evaluation of such models. However, future studies should determine whether the additional complexity provides clinically meaningful improvements beyond simpler and more interpretable approaches. Openly available models and reusable glucose representations could further reduce the resources required to investigate these approaches and enable researchers to adapt pretrained models to smaller, task-specific datasets. Nevertheless, open access alone does not ensure generalizability, particularly if the underlying training data do not adequately represent the populations in which the models are intended to be used in.

title: 7  Future perspectives
section: 7.3 Fairness in Future Clinical Risk Prediction
text:
7.3 Fairness in Future Clinical Risk Prediction
Future efforts to develop and implement models for cardiovascular risk prediction should consider the diversity of the intended target population from the beginning. Adequate representation of racial, ethnic, and other minority groups is important not only during model development and external validation but also when evaluating clinical impact. A model exhibiting performance disparities across groups may reinforce existing healthcare inequities, particularly when underrepresentation in the training data reflects unequal access to care or health technologies. In such cases, the model may perform least effectively for groups that are already underserved, further limiting their opportunity to benefit from its implementation. Fairness assessments should therefore consider not only whether predictive performance differs across groups but also whether all groups can access and benefit from the intervention and whether its implementation reduces or reinforces existing healthcare inequities. These considerations should be guided by the characteristics and healthcare context of the intended population and revisited throughout model development, external evaluation, implementation, and post-deployment monitoring.

title: English Abstract
text:
Background
Diabetes is characterized by chronic high blood glucose levels and is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Current CVD risk prediction in diabetes relies largely on traditional risk factors and HbA1c, although these measures may not fully capture clinically relevant glucose dynamics. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) provides detailed information on glucose variability, time in range (TIR), and short-term glucose fluctuations, and recent advances in machine learning offer new opportunities to learn directly from CGM data.


Aim
The aim was to evaluate the role of CGM data and machine learning approaches in cardiovascular risk assessment and examined potential fairness concerns in CGM-based prediction models.


Methods
The dissertation comprised three studies. Study I was a scoping review of the literature on CGM-derived metrics and CVD risk assessment. Study II investigated representations from the CGMformer foundation model and assessed whether CGM data could improve prediction of NT-proBNP, a biomarker indicative of heart failure risk. Study III examined racial group fairness in 60-minute blood glucose forecasting using long-short term memory models and CGM data from an American cohort.


Results
Study I found that the current evidence was inconsistent and heterogeneous. Most studies investigated subclinical cardiovascular outcomes. Studies including people with T2D were more frequent than studies including people with T1D (34/53 vs. 20/53), and the T2D study populations were generally larger. This pattern was observed both for TIR (median [IQR]: 510 [405–600] vs. 214 [119–547]) and mean amplitude of glycemic excursions (MAGE) (251 [89–411] vs. 57 [30–215]). Although TIR and MAGE were the most frequently studied CGM-derived metrics, only MAGE had been evaluated for CVD prediction, showing modest discriminatory performance (AUROC: ~0.61).
Study II showed that embeddings from the CGMformer foundation model captured both long-term and short-term glycemic patterns, related to HbA1c and TIR. Cosine distances further indicated that CGM embeddings from days belonging to the same participant were more similar to each other than embeddings from different participants. This was observed in both CANCAN (median [IQR]: within-participant, 0.058 [0.040–0.084] vs. between-participant, 0.117 [0.076–0.182]) and T1DX (within-participant, 0.064 [0.047–0.090] vs. between-participant, 0.082 [0.057–0.122]). However, the CGMformer embeddings did not improve prediction of NT-proBNP when added to a model including clinical variables selected based on the SCORE2-Diabetes risk score. Similarly, adding TIR and MAGE only modestly changed performance (corrected AUROC [95% CI]: SCORE2-Diabetes, 0.79 [0.76–0.87] vs. SCORE2-Diabetes + TIR + MAGE, 0.81 [0.77–0.88]). A simpler model including age alone already showed good discriminatory performance (corrected AUROC 0.73 [95% CI: 0.65–0.80]).
Study III found performance differences across racial groups in 60-minute blood glucose forecasting, even though the models were developed using only CGM data. Although the RMSE slope across training-set compositions was not statistically significant within either racial group, the difference in slopes between groups was statistically significant (\(p\) = 0.02). Meaning that when the training data composition changed from 0% White and 100% Black participants to 100% White and 0% Black participants, RMSE increased by 0.04 [95% CI: 0.01, 0.08] mmol/L more for Black participants than for White participants. After transfer learning, this difference was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (0.02 [95% CI: -0.01 to 0.05] mmol/L, \(p\) = 0.20).


Conclusion
Overall, the findings suggest that CGM data contains clinically meaningful information and may contribute to cardiovascular risk assessment for people with diabetes in the future. However, its current predictive value appears limited, particularly when compared with established demographic and clinical markers. While CGM-derived metrics such as TIR and MAGE may provide useful information, CGM foundation model embeddings did not improve prediction of NT-proBNP despite capturing relevant glycemic structure. Larger and more diverse datasets may provide better opportunities to use machine learning methods to fully exploit the temporal information contained in CGM data. Finally, the dissertation highlights the importance of evaluating generalizability and fairness when developing machine learning models based on CGM data, particularly for models intended for clinical use.

title: Dansk Resumé
text:
Introduktion
Diabetes er karakteriseret ved kronisk forhøjede glukoseniveauer og er associeret med en øget risiko for udvikling af hjertekarsygdomme. Nuværende modeller til prædiktion af hjertekarsygdomme bygger hovedsageligt på traditionelle risikofaktorer og HbA1c, selvom disse mål ikke fuldt ud fanger klinisk relevante glukosefluktuationer. Kontinuerlige glukosemålere (CGM) giver en detaljeret beskrivelse af glukosevariabilitet, tid i målområdet (TIR) og kortsigtede glukoseudsving. Samtidig har udviklingen inden for maskinlæring åbnet nye muligheder for at lære direkte fra CGM-data.


Formål
Formålet med denne afhandling var at evaluere rollen af CGM-data og maskinlæringsmetoder i prædiktion af kardiovaskulær risiko samt at undersøge potentielle fairness-udfordringer i CGM-baserede prædiktionsmodeller.


Metode
Afhandlingen består af tre studier. Studie I var et scoping review om CGM-afledte mål og kardiovaskulær risiko og prædiktion. Studie II undersøgte lærte repræsentationer fra foundation-modellen CGMformer og evaluerede, om CGM-data kunne forbedre prædiktionen af NT-proBNP. Studie III undersøgte, om en model til prædiktion af glukoseniveauet 60 minutter frem i tiden havde forskellig prædiktiv ydeevne på tværs af to grupper baseret på race.


Resultater.
Studie I viste, at den nuværende evidens var inkonsistent og heterogen. De fleste studier undersøgte CGM-data i relation til subkliniske hjertekarsygdomme. Studier med personer med T2D var hyppigere end studier med personer med T1D (34/53 vs. 20/53), og T2D-studiepopulationerne var generelt større. Dette mønster blev observeret for både tid i målområdet (TIR) (median [IQR]: 510 [405–600] vs. 214 [119–547]) og mean amplitude of glycemic excursions (MAGE; gennemsnitlig amplitude af glykæmiske udsving) (251 [89–411] vs. 57 [30–215]). Kun MAGE var blevet undersøgt som prædiktor for hjertekarsygdomme, og den prædiktive ydeevne var beskeden (AUROC: ca. 0.61).
Studie II viste, at lærte repræsentationer fra CGMformer kunne opfange både langsigtede og kortsigtede glukosemønstre relateret til HbA1c og TIR. Cosineafstandene indikerede desuden, at lærte repræsentationer fra dage tilhørende samme deltager var mere ens end repræsentationer fra dage tilhørende forskellige deltagere. Dette mønster blev observeret i både CANCAN-datasættet (median [IQR]: samme deltager, 0.058 [0.040–0.084] vs. forskellige deltagere, 0.117 [0.076–0.182]) og T1DX-datasættet (samme deltager, 0.064 [0.047–0.090] vs. forskellige deltagere, 0.082 [0.057–0.122]).
De lærte repræsentationer forbedrede ikke prædiktionen af NT-proBNP, når de blev tilføjet til modeller, der allerede inkluderede kliniske variable udvalgt på baggrund af SCORE2-Diabetes modellen. Tilsvarende gav tilføjelsen af TIR og MAGE kun en beskeden ændring i resultaterne (korrigeret AUROC [95% CI]: SCORE2-Diabetes, 0.79 [0.76–0.87] vs. SCORE2-Diabetes + TIR + MAGE, 0.81 [0.77–0.88]). Allerede før CGM-data blev tilføjet, havde modeller baseret på kliniske variable god prædiktiv ydeevne. En simpel model, der kun inkluderede alder, havde en korrigeret AUROC på 0.73 [95% CI: 0.65–0.80].
Studie III viste forskelle i prædiktiv ydeevne på tværs af racemæssige grupper ved prædiktion af glukoseniveauet 60 minutter frem i tiden, selvom modellerne udelukkende var trænet på CGM-data. Forskellen mellem grupperne var statistisk signifikant (\(p\) = 0.02), selvom RMSE-hældningen på tværs af træningssæt med forskellig racemæssig sammensætning ikke var statistisk signifikant inden for hver gruppe. Det vil sige at når træningsdatasammensætningen ændrede sig fra 0% ikke-hispanisk hvide deltagere og 100% ikke-hispanisk sorte deltagere til 100% ikke-hispanisk hvide deltagere og 0% ikke-hispanisk sorte deltagere, steg RMSE med 0.04 mmol/L mere for ikke-hispanisk sorte deltagere end for ikke-hispanisk hvide deltagere (95% CI: 0.01, 0.08). Efter transfer learning var denne signifikante forskel i prædiktiv ydeevne ikke længere til stede (0.02 mmol/L [95% CI: -0.01, 0.05], \(p\) = 0.20).


Konklusion
Samlet set tyder fundene på, at CGM-data indeholder klinisk meningsfuld information og potentielt kan bidrage til fremtidig prædiktion af kardiovaskulær risiko hos personer med diabetes. Den nuværende diskriminative ydeevne er dog beskeden sammenlignet med etablerede demografiske og kliniske markører. TIR og MAGE kan bidrage med relevant information, men lærte repræsentationer fra foundation-modellen CGMformer forbedrede ikke prædiktionen af NT-proBNP, selvom repræsentationerne indeholdt relevante glukosemønstre.
Større og mere diverse datasæt kan muligvis forbedre anvendelsen af maskinlæring og dermed udnytte det fulde potentiale i temporale CGM-data. Endelig fremhæver afhandlingen vigtigheden af at evaluere generaliserbarhed og fairness under udviklingen af CGM-baserede maskinlæringsmodeller, særligt når modellerne er tiltænkt klinisk anvendelse.
